summary: For ages 7-9 (Lower KS2/Grades 2-4), learners apply a checkable body-plan rule — an adult insect has 6 legs and 3 body parts — to sort minibeasts into 'insect' and 'not insect', then into finer groups (arachnid, crustacean, other). The core move is reasoning FROM a counted feature ('8 legs and 2 body parts, so it's an arachnid like a spider — not an insect') rather than by appearance, size, or how 'creepy' a creature looks. The activity confronts the dominant 'spiders/worms/woodlice are all insects' misconception head-on, using counting as the corrective.
misconceptions: 'Spiders are insects' — the dominant error; spiders have 8 legs and 2 body parts (arachnids).
'Anything small and crawly is an insect' — treating 'insect' as a synonym for bug/minibeast.
'Worms and snails are insects' — they lack the six-legs/three-parts plan entirely.
'Woodlice are insects' — they are crustaceans with 14 legs.
Sorting by size, colour or scariness instead of by counted features.

activities.title: Is it an insect? Sort-and-count
steps: Take a mixed set of real minibeast photos (e.g. ant, beetle, spider, woodlouse, worm, snail) and two bins labelled INSECT and NOT AN INSECT.
Before placing each creature, count its legs and its body parts — touching or marking each leg as you count so you don't miss any.
Place the creature in a bin and say the reason aloud in the form: 'It has ___ legs and ___ body parts, so it is / is not an insect.'
Check the spider carefully: count all 8 legs and notice its body is in 2 parts; place it in NOT AN INSECT and name it an arachnid.

Check the woodlouse (14 legs) and the worm (no legs) the same way. Handle the snail as a clear non-insect 'other': it has no legs (a shell and one muscular foot), so it fails the six-legs test — do not try to fit it to a leg-count group. Confirm the beetle and ant have 6 legs and 3 parts and belong in INSECT.
Expert round: re-sort into four bins — insect / arachnid / crustacean / other — and justify each placement by its distinguishing feature.
activities.insight: Classification means grouping by a definite, countable feature, not by appearance. An insect is defined by 6 legs and 3 body parts; creatures that fail this test (spider 8 legs/2 parts, woodlouse 14 legs, worm no legs, snail no legs/shell+foot) belong to other groups.

activities.title: Comparison plate: features side by side
steps: Study a side-by-side plate of an insect, a spider, a woodlouse, and a worm.
For each creature, reveal or record its leg count and number of body parts (tap-to-reveal counts work if the plate is interactive).

Fill in a feature-to-group link for the creatures on the plate: 6 legs and 3 body parts → insect, 8 legs and 2 body parts → arachnid, woodlouse with 14 legs → crustacean, no legs → worm/other. (Having many legs does not by itself make an animal a crustacean: centipedes and millipedes have many legs but are not crustaceans.)
State what makes each group different in one sentence.
activities.insight: Each minibeast group has a distinguishing observable feature; seeing the counts side by side makes the contrasts explicit before sorting new cases.

activities.title: The spider sets the record straight
steps: Act out or read a short exchange in which a spider objects: 'I'm NOT an insect — count my legs!'
Respond by actually counting the spider's legs (8) and body parts (2) and stating the group it belongs to.

Discuss a stage-vs-group counterexample: a caterpillar looks worm-like but is the young stage of an insect that becomes a butterfly or moth. Treat this as a discussion of life stage versus group only — not as a leg-counting case, since a caterpillar's prolegs can make a raw leg count misleading.
Discuss: could something be tiny and live in the garden and STILL not be an insect? Give an example (spider, worm, woodlouse, snail).
activities.insight: Surfacing the misconception in role makes the learner defend or reject 'insect' with the counted feature rather than with a feeling about what counts as a 'bug'.

activities.title: Explain-your-decision check
steps: Someone put a spider in the 'insect' box — decide whether that is right.
Sort these four — spider, ant, woodlouse, worm — into 'insect' and 'not insect'.
For each one, say HOW you decided (which feature you counted).
Answer the follow-ups: give the one feature that proves the spider is out; say whether a 14-legged woodlouse is an insect and which rule tells you.
activities.insight: Being able to state the deciding feature for each creature distinguishes a learner who owns the six-legs/three-parts rule from one relying on 'it's small and creepy'.

checkQuestion: Someone put a spider in the 'insect' box. Is that right? Sort these for me — spider, ant, woodlouse, worm — into 'insect' and 'not insect', and each time tell me HOW you decided.
checkAnswer: The spider is NOT an insect — it has 8 legs and 2 body parts (it's an arachnid). Only the ant is an insect (6 legs, 3 body parts). The woodlouse (14 legs) and the worm (no legs) are also not insects. The deciding rule is the six-legs test: an insect has exactly six legs and three body parts; anything else is 'not insect'.
